topic: Wake: Every Coding-Agent Session on Your Mac in One Place
summary: Wake (iAmCorey/Wake) is a native macOS app, built in Rust with GPUI (Zed's UI framework), that reads the local session history of 22 coding agents - Claude Code, Codex CLI, Cursor, OpenCode, Gemini CLI, Qodo/Qoder, Copilot CLI, Kiro, Pi, Oh My Pi, Grok Build, Kimi Code, Antigravity CLI, DeepSeek Harness, Hermes Agent, OpenClaw, CodeBuddy, WorkBuddy, ZCode, Craft Agents, Devin and OpenCode 2 - into one read-only SQLite FTS5 index, with trigram search, transcript rendering, one-click resume in Terminal/iTerm, an SSH remote-host mirror, and a bundled read-only MCP server plus CLI so other agents can query the history themselves. Verified 2026-09-28: 1,374 stars, 87 forks, 5 open issues, MIT licensed, Rust, created 2026-08-18, 42 releases from v0.1.0 (2026-08-19) to v0.8.5 (2026-09-27), 2,593 cumulative release-asset downloads, 68 commits in the last two weeks, macOS 14+ universal binary, ad-hoc signed (Gatekeeper blocks first launch), and still no Homebrew cask. The real story is the second product inside it: wake-mcp and wake-cli turn a personal session archive into shared context that any agent can read, which is the part that separates Wake from a crowded field of viewer tools.

app.name: Wake
app.author: iAmCorey
app.language: Rust (2,517,165 bytes); also Python 34,869, Shell 11,264, PowerShell 2,483, Swift 1,169
app.min_os: macOS 14 (Sonoma)+ for the primary build; Linux experimental since v0.2.5, Windows experimental since v0.2.7
app.packaging: Universal Binary (Apple Silicon + Intel) macOS .zip; .deb and tar.gz for Linux amd64/arm64; .zip for Windows x86_64
app.signing: ad-hoc signed, not notarized - Gatekeeper blocks the first launch; README recommends right-click Open or `xattr -d com.apple.quarantine Wake.app`; Windows binary is unsigned, so SmartScreen may block
install: Download Wake-<version>-macos.zip from GitHub Releases, unzip, drag Wake to Applications
Build from source: git clone https://github.com/iAmCorey/Wake && cd Wake && scripts/make-app.sh (add --universal for the Intel+ARM build)
Linux: .deb or tar.gz with a user-level install.sh (no root)
app.homebrew: no cask exists as of 2026-09-28 - Homebrew formulae API returns nothing for 'wake' and open issue #6 requests a Brew formula
app.index_location: ~/Library/Application Support/wake/wake.db (Linux ~/.local/share/wake, Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\wake); rebuildable from scratch, with stars/pins kept in a separate table that survives rebuilds
app.ui: GPUI 0.2 + gpui-component 0.5 - the same UI framework as Zed; three-pane workbench with a ⌘K / Ctrl+K command palette

list: Cursor (~/.cursor/projects/**/agent-transcripts plus the IDE Chat/Composer store state.vscdb)
OpenCode 2 / opencode2 (opencode.db and opencode-next.db, session_v2 tables)
Antigravity CLI (metadata only - transcripts are encrypted)
DeepSeek Harness / dsh (~/.dsh/sessions/**/session[.vN].jsonl[.zstd], zstd decoded transparently)
WorkBuddy (~/.workbuddy/projects/*/*.jsonl, WORKBUDDY_CONFIG_DIR respected; desktop app, no resume)
ZCode (~/.zcode/cli/db/db.sqlite + v2/tasks-index.sqlite, ZCODE_STORAGE_DIR respected; desktop app, no resume)
Craft Agents (~/.craft-agent/workspaces/*/sessions/*/session.jsonl; desktop app, no resume)
agents_supported.explicitly_unsupported: Windsurf and Trae (local data encrypted), Amp, Factory (Droid) and Warp (sessions kept in the cloud), Reasonix (local but not yet mapped)
agents_supported.metadata_caveats: The README's Model column (whether Wake can show which LLM a session used) is only filled for some agents; the Via column (CLI vs IDE extension vs desktop app) is filled for Codex, Hermes, OpenClaw and Craft Agents only. A dash means the agent's own local data does not record the field, not that Wake lacks the feature - a distinction most competing tools paper over.

mcp_server.transport: stdio, hand-written JSON-RPC, read-only over Wake's index
tools: wake_search - full-text search across titles and transcripts, returns wake://session/<key>#<seq> references
wake_list_sessions - recent sessions scoped by project, agent, time window or starred
wake_get_session - one transcript as compact Markdown with [seq N] markers, paginated via from_seq
wake_list_projects - projects with indexed sessions, most recently active first
wake_list_memories - the memory files agents keep for themselves, grouped by project
mcp_server.setup: Settings → Connect shows copy-paste snippets; e.g. `claude mcp add --scope user wake -- "/Applications/Wake.app/Contents/MacOS/wake-mcp"`, or a [mcp_servers.wake] block in ~/.codex/config.toml; `wake-mcp setup` prints them from a terminal

cli.binary: wake-cli, prints byte-identical output to the MCP tools (asserted in the test suite apart from a trailing newline)
commands: wake-cli refresh (keeps the index fresh from a scheduled task while the app is closed)
cli.skill: `npx skills add iAmCorey/Wake` installs a bundled agent skill, and docs/cli.md documents a Claude Code SessionStart hook that injects the project's recent sessions at startup

other_features.search: SQLite FTS5 trigram index; matches CJK text and code substrings like `useEffect(`; opens the transcript at the matched message; results favour recently active sessions; titles are searched too, with title hits first
other_features.transcript_view: per-message user/assistant bubbles, inline images (copy or save through the system Save dialog), collapsible tool-call clusters, thinking summaries, tree-sitter highlighting for 30+ languages
other_features.resume: one click reopens the session in Terminal/iTerm at the original project directory (claude --resume, codex resume, ...); Linux and Windows use native terminal hosts
other_features.insights: GitHub-style activity heatmap with streaks, hour/weekday/month breakdowns, and Agents/Projects/Models leaderboards switchable between sessions, tokens and prompts; plus an 'Agents asking Wake' board showing how often each agent used Wake's MCP tools or CLI in the last 7 days
other_features.memory_page: added in v0.8.0 - Claude Code auto-memory, Codex memories and per-session summaries, ZCode project memory, and the instruction files you write (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, GEMINI.md, .cursor/rules, .kiro/steering, copilot-instructions.md) in one searchable read-only place
other_features.cleanup: session cleanup from the sidebar (filter by date/agent/project, sort by size, preview, then move files to Trash with a tombstone so deleted sessions stay deleted), with cleanup history
other_features.remote_hosts: mirror other machines' sessions over SSH/rsync into remotes/<host>/ under Wake's own data dir; sessions get an @host badge and resume via a copied `ssh -t <host> 'cd <project> && codex resume <id>'` command; requires promptless SSH keys and rsync on both ends; remote sessions are read-only and Windows remotes are unsupported
other_features.handoff: Copy Handoff (v0.8.0) copies a ready-to-paste note with the session id and both ways to read it, for handing a conversation to another agent
other_features.language: follows the system language on first launch, falls back to English; Simplified Chinese ships with the app; adding a language is one flat JSON file accepted as a PR

competitors.title: ctx - Instant recall for coding agents. Search the history already on your machine (ctxrs/ctx, site ctx.rs)
key_points: The most direct rival by traction and intent: 1,140 stars, 71 forks, Apache-2.0, Rust, created 2026-02-23, still pushing on 2026-09-28 - roughly the same audience as Wake but CLI-first, not a GUI

Pitch is 'git blame, but for agent sessions': ctx search finds the session, ctx show retrieves the exact event, ctx locate says where it came from, and ctx blame maps lines of code back to the session that produced them
Explicitly positions against 'agent memory' products: 'ctx gives agents instant recall of the real record without a lossy memory step' - the same transcript-not-summary argument Wake makes

Ships three more surfaces Wake has no answer for: ctx graph (codebase relationship mapping), ctx sift (cuts noisy tool output before the agent reads it), and BM25 lexical plus locally-computed semantic search with no vector database
Claims 50x better token efficiency than raw transcript search; default lexical search stays available while the local embedding model builds, and no API key is needed
Understands parent sessions, subagents and forks so agents can recover a whole chain of work - the same relationship modelling Wake does for Grok Build subagents and Codex spawn_agent threads

Its Show HN thread reached 65 points and 43 comments (2026-07-02) even as the discussion derailed into an argument about AI-generated comments; the top genuine thread was the author's call for a standard agent-transcript format
One-click install by prompt or `curl -fsSL https://ctx.rs/install | sh`; cross-platform on macOS, Linux and Windows PowerShell

competitors.title: Sessio - a desktop workspace for coding agents (LarchLiu/sessio)
key_points: The clearest product-level alternative: 28 stars, 2 forks, TypeScript, created 2026-05-12, last pushed 2026-09-13, no license file

Does the same browsing job as Wake - SQLite index over Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode and external Pi sessions, file watching, project grouping, markdown/KaTeX/diff rendering, subagent support, rename and delete - but adds live agent chat over the Agent Client Protocol

Where it goes past Wake: it can start and continue sessions inside the app, stream text/reasoning/tool calls, answer permission prompts in-chat, pick model/reasoning effort/permission mode, and fork a session to a different agent while carrying context across - Wake deliberately never runs an agent
Connects the same runtime to Telegram and other IM channels, so agents are reachable from a chat app; Wake's remote story is SSH mirroring, not interaction
Evidence that the category is converging on 'browser plus runner' while Wake has staked out 'browser plus agent-readable index'

competitors.title: Session Manager - browse, search, inspect, archive and clean up local and remote AI coding-agent sessions (CatheadOwl/session-manager)
key_points: 10 stars, 2 forks, MIT, Rust behind a Tauri v2 + React 18 shell, created 2026-07-21, last pushed 2026-09-20; explicitly inspired by CC Switch's session browser
Cross-platform by construction (Windows, macOS, Linux) where Wake is macOS-first with experimental Linux and Windows ports - the same capability gap from the opposite direction

Three-column workspace centred on fork trees: branching views of sessions that share prompt history, which is a sharper answer to 'which of these near-identical sessions is the one I want' than a flat list
Read-only remote SSH sources are a first-class setting rather than a mirror feature, and there is no resume step - it is an inspector and archivist, not a launcher
Low adoption relative to Wake, but it demonstrates that the basic scan-index-search loop is no longer a differentiator in this niche

competitors.title: Session Explorer - local web app for browsing Claude Code and Codex CLI session histories (prime-radiant-inc/claude-session-viewer)
key_points: 43 stars, TypeScript, created 2026-02-04, last pushed 2026-06-09, no license - the most-starred of the older wave of viewers and now visibly stalled

Delivery model is the opposite of Wake's: a local web app (React Router + Express + SQLite) you open in a browser rather than a native window, which sidesteps GPUI/platform work but loses the one-click terminal resume
Covers only Claude Code and Codex CLI - the two sources that account for most users, and the subset every competitor starts with
Illustrates the maintenance trap Wake has to avoid: session formats are private implementation details of tools on their own release cadence, so a viewer that stops shipping stops working

competitors.title: codex-history-viewer - VS Code extension for Codex CLI and Claude Code session history (HizTam/codex-history-viewer)
key_points: 39 stars, MIT, TypeScript, created 2026-01-20, still pushing on 2026-09-28 - the most actively maintained competitor after ctx
A different form factor: lives inside VS Code, browses/searches/tags/imports/exports history and resumes a session in the related VS Code extension instead of a terminal
Its differentiators are tagging and import/export of session history - portability of the archive, which Wake only offers as Markdown export
Shows the category splitting by editor gravity: users who never leave the IDE, versus Wake's assumption that agent work happens in a terminal

competitors.title: session-indexer - per-project semantic search over Claude Code session history (valpere/session-indexer)
key_points: 42 stars, Go, Apache-2.0, created 2026-06-25, last pushed 2026-09-27
Indexes JSONL transcripts into SQLite and retrieves via bge-m3 embeddings through Ollama, with FTS5 as the fallback - the semantic-search counterargument to Wake's pure lexical trigram index
Scoped per project rather than global, which narrows the corpus and improves precision but cannot answer 'which project was that in?'
Claude Code only; like most rivals it is a single-agent tool and therefore has no answer for the multi-agent case that motivates Wake

competitors.title: Universal Session Viewer - Electron desktop app for Claude Code transcripts (tad-hq/universal-session-viewer)
key_points: 18 stars, AGPL-3.0, TypeScript/Electron, created 2025-12-23, last pushed 2026-03-23 - six months stale
Features continuation chain detection and AI-powered session summaries, i.e. it summarises rather than only indexing, which ctx explicitly argues against
AGPL-3.0 versus Wake's MIT - a licensing difference that matters to anyone embedding the tool in a company workflow
The Electron footprint is the trade-off Wake avoids by building on GPUI, at the cost of a macOS-first platform matrix

competitors.title: What is Wake: All Your Code Agent Sessions in One Desktop App (4Geeks, Aug 30 2026)
key_points: The most detailed third-party explainer: walks through the per-agent storage paths (Claude Code ~/.claude/projects, Codex ~/.codex/sessions plus SQLite, Qoder ~/.qoder/projects) before describing Wake as the unification layer
States the discovery problem precisely: 'this fragmentation forces developers to remember which agent they used for each task and navigate hidden directories to retrieve lost context'

Quotes the performance baseline (about 310 sessions / 800 MB of JSONL indexed in roughly five seconds, instant subsequent launches via mtime incremental scanning) and the sub-millisecond search target
Confirms the read-only guarantee in its FAQ - Wake never writes to agent databases or JSONL files, only indexes into its own local database
Records a growth point: 684 GitHub stars 'just weeks after its public launch' (2026-08-30) versus 1,374 on 2026-09-28

competitors.title: Claude Code Session Manager: Wake for Mac (Zentor Blog, 2026)
key_points: Frames Wake specifically as a Claude Code session manager for searches like 'claude code session manager' even though it indexes 13+ agents - the SEO framing a Wake review should correct

Best articulation of why transcripts matter: 'The commit message says what changed; the session says why the first two approaches didn't work, which library version broke, and what the error text actually was. Losing that isn't losing a chat log, it's losing the debugging.'
Praises the support table for being honest about gaps instead of claiming universal coverage, and calls out the Model/Via dash convention as 'a distinction most tools would quietly hide'
Confirms the macOS 14+ requirement and that there is no signed installer yet, plus the FAQ answers on read-only access and where Wake's own index lives
Says Wake 'was released on August 19, 2026' - consistent with v0.1.0 shipping the day after the repo was created

competitors.title: Wake pulls sessions from 15 coding agents into one searchable desktop app (reveneau, Sep 3 2026)
key_points: Reports 731 stars and 48 forks on 2026-09-03 - the mid-point of the growth curve between 4Geeks' 684 and today's 1,374

Frames the team case rather than the solo case: 'for a team where different engineers standardise on different agents, it is also the first place a session done in one tool becomes searchable by someone who does not use that tool'
Notes SSH session mirroring, model information for most agents, and the search/return latency under a millisecond on the author's ~310-session benchmark

Names the core strategic risk plainly: Wake is at 0.2 (at the time) and depends on the transcript formats of 15 tools 'that change on their own schedules, so the index can drift when an agent releases a new version'

competitors.title: Open-Source Wake Unifies Claude Code and Gemini CLI Histories on macOS (AlphaSignal, 2026)
key_points: Summarises the architecture accurately: Rust on GPUI, a wake-core data layer with a per-agent adapter trait, and normalisation of every format into one local SQLite index with incremental file-watch updates
Reports roughly 780 stars 'within a few weeks of release' and restates the MIT licence and macOS-only constraint
Highlights the read-only, zero-network-request posture as the trust argument a review should verify rather than repeat

competitors.title: Wake - All Coding-Agent Sessions in One macOS App (arsentev.ai GitHub radar)
key_points: Earliest datapoint in the growth curve: 352 stars, described as gathering sessions from 11 agents (the agent count has since grown to 22)
Publishes the performance numbers as headline claims: full index ~5s on a 310-session / 800 MB JSONL dataset, instant relaunch via mtime incremental scan, sub-millisecond search
States the value proposition for switchers - 'if you switch between Claude Code, Codex, and other agents daily, finding a specific past conversation across 11 different directories wastes real time'

Notable install advice for the audience: it suggests telling your own agent to install Wake from the repo and remove the quarantine flag if macOS blocks it - onboarding by handing the task to an agent

competitors.title: Hacker News coverage check for Wake (2026-09-28)
key_points: Zero Hacker News submissions and zero comment mentions found for iAmCorey/Wake or its URL - the launch did not go through HN at all, in contrast with ctx's 65-point Show HN thread

Wake's distribution is instead GitHub trending plus a long tail of aggregator and review sites, which is why the star count moved 352 → 684 → 731 → 780 → 1,374 in about four weeks while almost nobody in the HN audience has argued about it

The near-identical neighbour problem on HN is worth noting for context: Show HN posts for Cass (3 points), 'Local-first history, search, and analytics for Claude Code and Codex' (4 points), Dexicon (3) and Darc (2) all sank without discussion

For a buyer this means there is little adversarial scrutiny of Wake's claims online - the review opportunity is to actually test the ones that matter (index drift after an agent update, remote mirror limits, Gatekeeper friction)

competitors.title: agentsview - Browse, search, and track costs across your AI coding agents (kenn-io/agentsview, site agentsview.io)
key_points: The category's population leader and the most important omission from most Wake coverage: 6,011 stars, 687 forks, MIT, Go, created 2026-02-19, latest release v0.44.0 on 2026-09-21, 108 open issues - roughly 4.4x Wake's star count.

Different architecture for the same job: a detached local daemon plus a web UI at 127.0.0.1:8080 and a desktop app (brew install --cask agentsview), with a Docker image - server-based against Wake's single native GPUI app.
Competes on analytics and cost rather than browsing: token totals, peak context tokens, and cost estimates priced via LiteLLM and OpenRouter rates with an offline fallback.
Deeper directory coverage in specific corners: Kiro IDE, legacy Kilo VS Code globalStorage, Goose, gptme, Crush per-project databases, Kimi Work desktop, Augure Desktop (v3 beta).

Its opt-in and deprecated adapters are the clearest independent evidence of the same local-data fragmentation Wake fights: Aider is opt-in because it needs a config path, and Amp support is deprecated because current Amp releases may keep threads in the cloud.

Privacy wording is meaningfully softer than Wake's: 'your session archive stays on your machine unless you choose a feature that shares it', because sharing features exist (sync, pg push, duckdb push).

competitors.title: CCManager - Coding Agent Session Manager for Claude Code / Gemini CLI / Codex CLI / Cursor Agent / Copilot CLI / Cline CLI / OpenCode / Kimi CLI (kbwo/ccmanager)
key_points: The top project that literally brands itself a 'Coding Agent Session Manager': 1,253 stars, TypeScript, pushed 2026-09-27 - so it wins the exact keyword this article targets even though it does a different job.

It does not index history at all: it launches and supervises live sessions, running multiple agents in parallel across git worktrees and multiple repositories from one self-contained interface with no tmux dependency.
Live state detection per CLI (busy / waiting / idle) with status-change hooks for notifications and automation - the operational visibility Wake does not attempt.
Worktree lifecycle inside the app, session restore after a crash, and copying Claude Code session data into new worktrees to carry conversation context across branches.

Devcontainer support and an experimental auto-approval path using a Haiku verifier, explicitly contrasted in its README against Claude Squad's AutoYes, which bypasses Claude Code's security confirmations.

Category-defining lesson for the article: 'session manager' names two different products - an archive you search (Wake, agentsview, cass, ctx) or a live run controller (ccmanager, Orca, Paseo, Agent of Empires).

competitors.title: coding-agent-search (cass) - Unified TUI and CLI to index and search local coding agent history (Dicklesworthstone/coding_agent_session_search)
key_points: 1,149 stars, 140 forks, Rust (pinned nightly), alpha, Linux/macOS/Windows, MIT plus an OpenAI/Anthropic rider, created 2025-11-21 and still pushed on 2026-09-28.

TUI and CLI rather than a GUI, and built for agents as first-class users: --robot and --json modes, a selftest command, and an explicit warning never to run bare cass in an agent context because it launches the interactive TUI.

Claims the widest provider list in the category, mixing CLI agents, IDE agents and cloud ones: Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Cline, OpenCode, Amp, Cursor, ChatGPT, Aider, Pi-Agent, Prime Agent, Oh My Pi, GitHub Copilot Chat, Copilot CLI, OpenClaw, Clawdbot, Vibe, Crush, Goose, Hermes, Kimi Code, Muse Code, Qwen Code, Factory Droid, Antigravity, OpenHands, Grok Build, Grok Bot, Codebuff, Devin CLI, Shelley and Kiro CLI.

Search is hybrid - lexical plus semantic - by default, with an explicit lexical mode and workspace/time scoping (--workspace, --days) that Wake does not offer: the answer to 'I know roughly what it was about, not what it said'.
Distribution is smoother than Wake's: Homebrew tap and Scoop bucket plus verified install scripts, though Intel macOS still requires building from source.
Its own candid limits are the useful counterweight: alpha status and a pinned nightly Rust toolchain, versus Wake's stable-toolchain Universal Binary.

competitors.title: agf - Find, search, and resume AI coding-agent sessions across Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build, Kiro and more (subinium/agf)
key_points: 154 stars, Rust, MIT, on crates.io with a Homebrew tap and prebuilt macOS/Linux/Windows binaries - a deliberately single-purpose fuzzy finder: 'Find the AI coding session you meant to resume.'
Resume-first rather than browse-first: one-key resume with a resume-mode picker, scanning for agent sessions locally rather than rendering full transcripts.
Independently reviewed alongside agentsview as the complementary pair - agentsview for retrospective 'what did I do this week' analytics, agf for 'pick up right where I left off' immediacy.
Useful category evidence for the article: demand is high enough that the niche has split into GUI archives, TUI resume finders, CLI/semantic search tools and live-run orchestrators.

stats.fact: iAmCorey/Wake had 1,374 stars, 87 forks, 5 open issues and 2 watchers on 2026-09-28, with the repo created 2026-08-18 and last pushed 2026-09-27
Wake is licensed MIT and written predominantly in Rust (2,517,165 bytes), with Python (34,869), Shell (11,264), PowerShell (2,483) and Swift (1,169) as supporting languages
Wake shipped 42 releases between v0.1.0 on 2026-08-19 and v0.8.5 on 2026-09-27 - a 39-day span, or roughly one release per day
Wake's release assets total 2,593 cumulative downloads; the macOS zip is the volume driver (67 for v0.8.4, 56 for v0.8.5) against 37/30 for Windows and single digits for each Linux asset
stats.source: sum of asset download_count across all releases, GitHub releases API

stats.fact: The repo saw 68 commits in the two weeks from 2026-09-14 to 2026-09-28, and 181 of all commits are by the sole author iAmCorey

Eight contributors appear in total: iAmCorey (181), 'claude' (10), YTwsy (3), and one commit each from bet4it, Tespera, MiQieR, BUKOWSKIREAL and yougeqiu - a single-maintainer project with an unusually high share of agent-authored commits

Wake has grown from 352 stars (arsentev.ai, early September) to 684 (4Geeks, 2026-08-30), 731 with 48 forks (reveneau, 2026-09-03), about 780 (AlphaSignal) and 1,374 (2026-09-28) - roughly a 4x increase in four weeks
stats.source: cross-source comparison against GitHub API on 2026-09-28

stats.fact: No Hacker News submission or comment mention of iAmCorey/Wake exists as of 2026-09-28 - the project's discovery happened through GitHub and aggregator coverage, not HN

Wake's README documents 22 supported agents, and the wake-core adapter directory confirms it with per-agent modules (claude, codex, qoder, copilot, cursor, cursor_ide, opencode, kiro, gemini, pi, omp, grok, grok_group, kimi, antigravity, dsh, hermes, openclaw, codebuddy, craft, devin, zcode plus shared parse_utils and sqlite_ro helpers)

Wake's own performance baseline is about 310 sessions and 800 MB of JSONL indexed in roughly 5 seconds, with instant subsequent launches via mtime-based incremental scanning and search results under 1 ms
Search uses SQLite FTS5 with a trigram index, which is what makes CJK text and code substrings like `useEffect(` searchable in the same query language

Wake's privacy stance is read-only agent directories, credential files such as auth.json never read, and no background network requests - the only network actions are a user-initiated GitHub update check and, if configured, SSH/rsync to remote hosts

The bundled MCP server exposes exactly five read-only tools (wake_search, wake_list_sessions, wake_get_session, wake_list_projects, wake_list_memories) and deliberately offers no delete or star tool; its one write is resolving the default index path inside Wake's own data directory

Wake's five open issues on 2026-09-28 are #56 (remote sync fails on Windows, rsync parses C:\ paths as a remote host), #55 (desktop-app hand-off, Warp tab resume, pi-web target), #52 (a Chinese-language request for full Antigravity IDE session records), #51 (adjustable font size / UI zoom) and #6 (provide a Homebrew formula)
No Homebrew cask for Wake exists: the formulae.brew.sh API returns no entry and Homebrew/homebrew-cask has no wake.rb, which is why open issue #6 asks for a Brew formula

Wake ships ad-hoc signed and not notarized, so macOS Gatekeeper blocks the first launch of a downloaded build; the README's workaround is right-click → Open or `xattr -d com.apple.quarantine Wake.app`, and Linux/Windows builds are similarly unsignged enough to trigger SmartScreen

wake-cli's output is asserted byte-for-byte against the MCP tools in the test suite, apart from one trailing newline the CLI adds - so an agent driving it over a shell sees what a connected MCP client sees

Wake understands the Codex background-thread problem: guardian auto-review, /review, compaction and memory-consolidation threads are skipped from metadata on the first line, spawn_agent sub-agents are kept and nested under their parent, and an unidentifiable file stays visible rather than risk hiding a real conversation (v0.6.6 and v0.8.0 changelog entries)

Wake handles the Craft Agents duplication problem: a Claude connection saves every conversation into Claude Code's history too, so Wake hides the engine copy while the Craft session exists and lets it reappear as a Claude Code session if the Craft session is deleted

JetBrains' 2026 Developer Ecosystem Survey (15,000+ professional developers, May-July 2026) found 90% using AI coding agents at work at least weekly and 68% daily, with Claude Code at 39% adoption at work (up from 18% in January 2026) and 47% in the US, Codex at 16% (up from 3%), and Cursor down to 12% from 18%

Multi-tool usage is now the norm, which is the entire premise of a session manager: 59% of developers use three or more AI programming tools, the average developer uses 2.3 at once (JetBrains AI Pulse, January 2026), and 70% of engineering teams pair Cursor with at least one other AI tool

A June 2026 survey of 40 working engineers found 65% routinely run two AI coding agents in tandem, with Cursor + Claude Code the most common pairing at 25% and the highest self-rated productivity of any setup tested - small sample, self-reported, but directionally aligned with the larger surveys

Agent-generated code share explains why transcripts matter: about 47% of work code is now fully written by agents, over half of developers write less than 20% of their code manually, and 22% generate more than 80% of their code with agents

The nearest rival by traction is ctx (ctxrs/ctx) at 1,140 stars, 71 forks, Apache-2.0, Rust, created 2026-02-23 and still actively pushed on 2026-09-28 - a CLI-first history search with code blame, graph mapping and tool-output sifting

Other session-history tools remain small: prime-radiant-inc/claude-session-viewer 43 stars (stalled since 2026-06-09), valpere/session-indexer 42, HizTam/codex-history-viewer 39, LarchLiu/sessio 28, tad-hq/universal-session-viewer 18, johnfkoo951/agent-archives 19 (last push 2026-01-12), CatheadOwl/session-manager 10, s-kolbusz/ai-memory-explorer 2, fucheng830/casr-gui 2

The category's largest project is not Wake: agentsview (kenn-io/agentsview) had 6,011 stars, 687 forks, 108 open issues and a v0.44.0 release dated 2026-09-21, roughly 4.4x Wake's 1,374 stars and with a release train running since February 2026

The most-starred project that literally calls itself a 'Coding Agent Session Manager' is CCManager (kbwo/ccmanager) at 1,253 stars - but it launches and supervises live sessions across git worktrees instead of indexing past transcripts, so it competes for the target keyword rather than the job Wake does

Agent-history search has fragmented into many small tools: cass 1,149 stars (Rust TUI with 30+ provider readers), getspecstory 1,341 stars, jhlee0409/claude-code-history-viewer 2,207 stars, session-knowledge 331 stars, agf 154 stars, valpere/session-indexer 42 stars, prime-radiant-inc/claude-session-viewer 43 stars

The adjacent live-orchestration tier dwarfs history search in adoption: stablyai/orca 80,570 stars, getpaseo/paseo 18,881 stars, agent-of-empires 3,298 stars - suggesting far more developers want to run many agents than to search old transcripts

Google autocomplete returns a full long-tail cluster for 'claude code history viewer' (windows, vscode, cchv, reddit, command, linux, github, cli, claude code session history viewer) and for 'claude code session' (list, limit, id, history, delete, plus Japanese 一覧 and 再開), but the exact target phrase 'coding agent session manager' returns no suggestions at all - the keyword is a positioning term with almost no discovery volume attached

angles: The second product is the real story: Wake ships wake-mcp (five read-only MCP tools) and wake-cli, so the session archive stops being something you browse and becomes context any agent can query - 'a new agent can pick up where another one left off'. Every rival viewer is a dead end for another agent; this is the part that changes how a workflow runs, and it is under-covered in the aggregator write-ups

Why transcripts are worth indexing at all - the single best framing to lead with: 'The commit message says what changed; the session says why the first two approaches didn't work, which library version broke, and what the error text actually was. Losing that isn't losing a chat log, it's losing the debugging.' git history is complete for code and empty for reasoning

22 agents is a maintenance liability, not just a feature list: Wake re-reads private, undocumented, tool-owned formats (JSONL and SQLite) that change on each agent's own release cadence. The changelog already shows the treadmill - DeepSeek Harness broke on dsh 0.1.6 and was fixed in 0.8.3, Cursor stopped writing token counts, Codex's background threads were being indexed as sessions until 0.6.6. The honest question is what happens after a format change and a lapsed maintainer

Read-only as the trust mechanism, and it is verifiable rather than marketing: agent directories opened read-only, auth.json and friends never read, stars/pins/tombstones in Wake's own DB, no background HTTP client, and an index at ~/Library/Application Support/wake/wake.db that can be rebuilt from scratch (with stars surviving rebuilds). Test it against your own ~/.claude before trusting it

FTS5 trigram is a specific, checkable design decision: it is why CJK text and code substrings like `useEffect(` both match, and why results can jump to the exact message instead of the file. The trade-off versus competitors running local embeddings (session-indexer with bge-m3, crispy-recall with vectors, ctx's optional semantic mode) is recall on paraphrased queries - Wake indexes the literal record and nothing else

Remote hosts over SSH is the honest feature and the biggest asterisk: it solves 'my other Mac/Linux box has the session', but remote sessions are read-only, cannot be trashed, need promptless SSH keys (Wake runs without a terminal and can never answer a passphrase prompt), need rsync on both ends, do not honour CODEX_HOME-style path overrides on the remote, and do not support Windows remotes. Issue #56 shows the first real-world failure, where a Windows local cache path is parsed as an SSH host

Insights is the unexpected feature: a GitHub-style heatmap with streaks, hour/weekday/month breakdowns, and Agents/Projects/Models leaderboards switchable between sessions, tokens and prompts - plus an 'Agents asking Wake' board measuring how often each agent used the MCP tools. That last board is a feedback loop: the tool reports whether agents actually adopted the tool

The Memory page is a quiet land grab worth explaining: v0.8.0 put CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, GEMINI.md, .cursor/rules, .kiro/steering and copilot-instructions.md next to each agent's own auto-memory in one searchable read-only view - so the app also answers 'what did I tell this agent, and did the other one get told the same thing?'

Gatekeeper friction is part of the onboarding and should be in the review, not the footnotes: ad-hoc signed, not notarized, so a downloaded build is blocked on first launch and needs right-click → Open or `xattr -d com.apple.quarantine Wake.app`. Add the missing Homebrew cask (open issue #6) and the install story is currently 'clone and build' or 'quarantine-flag your way in'

Zero Hacker News presence is itself a finding: 352 → 1,374 stars in four weeks with no HN thread and no adversarial discussion, while the near-identical Show HNs for Cass, Dexicon, Darc and a generic local-first history tool sank at 2-4 points. The claims circulating about Wake are unexamined, which is exactly where a hands-on review earns its place

The honest limitations section writes itself from the README: macOS 14+ only for the good build (Linux v0.2.5 and Windows v0.2.7 are experimental, with desktop integration explicitly less tested), Windsurf/Trae unsupported because they encrypt local data, Amp/Factory Droid/Warp unsupported because sessions live in the cloud, and Antigravity CLI indexed at metadata level only because its transcripts are encrypted. Also Craft Agents, WorkBuddy and ZCode are desktop apps, so they index but cannot be resumed

The market argument, with numbers: 59% of developers now run three or more AI programming tools and the average is 2.3, Claude Code is at 39% adoption at work and Codex went 3% → 16% in six months. Sessions are therefore spread across at least two tools by default, which turns 'which tool did I solve this in?' into a recurring weekly cost - and is the reason this niche has a dozen entrants in six months

Hermes Agent is one of the 22 adapters (~/.hermes/state.db plus profiles/*/state.db with HERMES_HOME respected), and it is one of the few where Wake can show which channel a session came in through. Worth flagging for a readership that runs Hermes locally: the same index that searches Claude Code can search your Hermes history

Position it against ctx rather than ignoring the CLI: a personal transcript index is now a crowded, cheap to build tool. The defensible parts are the 22 adapters, the resume flow that puts you back in a real terminal at the right directory, and the MCP/CLI surface - not the SQLite FTS5 search box, which at least nine other projects already have

Do not let one launch post define the comparison. agentsview has ~4.4x Wake's stars, a daemon plus web UI and cost analytics; cass has a wider provider list plus hybrid semantic search on Homebrew and Scoop; ctx has 'git blame for agent sessions'; ccmanager owns the literal 'session manager' keyword by running live agents in worktrees rather than indexing history. Wake's actual claim is narrower and defensible: the most polished native Mac window into that history, with zero network and the best cross-agent hand-off plumbing.

The target keyword has almost no search discovery behind it. Google autocomplete for the exact phrase 'coding agent session manager' returns nothing, while 'claude code history viewer' and 'claude code session' return dense long-tail clusters including Windows, VS Code, Linux, delete and Japanese 一覧/再開 queries. Write the headline and H2s for the queries people actually type, and use the target phrase as the category definition rather than the promise.

faq.q: Is Wake free and open source?
faq.a: Yes on both counts. The repository (github.com/iAmCorey/Wake) is MIT licensed and the prebuilt binaries are free to download, in contrast with tools in this niche that ship AGPL-3.0 or PolyForm Noncommercial terms.

faq.q: Does Wake replace Claude Code, Codex or Cursor?
faq.a: No. It never runs an agent and never supplies a model. It reads what those tools already wrote to disk, indexes it, and can reopen a session in your terminal with the agent's own resume command (claude --resume, codex resume, ...). Sessio is the rival that does run agents over ACP; Wake deliberately does not.

faq.q: Does Wake modify my Claude Code, Codex or Cursor files?
faq.a: No. Every agent directory is opened read-only and Wake never writes to another tool's files or databases. Credential files such as auth.json are never read. Stars, pins and delete-tombstones live in Wake's own index at ~/Library/Application Support/wake/wake.db, which can be rebuilt from scratch without losing them.

faq.q: Does Wake send anything over the network?
faq.a: Not in the background. The only network actions are a user-initiated update check against Wake's public GitHub Release metadata, and SSH/rsync to remote hosts if you configure them. Session data is never sent anywhere else.

faq.q: Which coding agents does Wake support?
faq.a: 22 as of v0.8.5: Claude Code, Codex CLI, Qoder CLI, Copilot CLI, Cursor (CLI transcripts plus IDE chat/composer history), OpenCode and OpenCode 2, Kiro, Gemini CLI, Pi, Oh My Pi, Grok Build, Kimi Code, Antigravity CLI (metadata only), DeepSeek Harness, Hermes Agent, OpenClaw, CodeBuddy, WorkBuddy, ZCode, Craft Agents and Devin.

faq.q: Why are Windsurf, Trae, Amp, Factory Droid and Warp missing?
faq.a: Windsurf and Trae encrypt their local data, and Amp, Factory (Droid) and Warp keep sessions in the cloud, so there is nothing local to read. Antigravity CLI is indexed at metadata level only for the same encryption reason. Reasonix stores sessions locally but has not been mapped yet.

faq.q: Does Wake run on Windows or Linux?
faq.a: macOS 14 or newer is the primary and best-supported platform, shipped as a Universal Binary for Apple Silicon and Intel. Linux support has been experimental since v0.2.5 and Windows since v0.2.7; the data layer, rendering and search are fully tested there, but terminal-resume targets and desktop integration have seen less real-desktop mileage.

faq.q: Can I install Wake with Homebrew?
faq.a: Not yet. There is no cask in Homebrew/homebrew-cask and the formulae API returns no 'wake' entry; open issue #6 requests a Brew formula. Today you download the macOS zip from Releases or build from source with a Rust toolchain.

faq.q: Why does macOS block Wake on first launch?
faq.a: The release is ad-hoc signed rather than notarized, so Gatekeeper refuses it. Right-click the app and choose Open, or run `xattr -d com.apple.quarantine Wake.app`. The Windows build is unsigned too and may trigger SmartScreen.

faq.q: How fast is Wake on a real history?
faq.a: The author's published baseline is about 310 sessions and 800 MB of JSONL indexed in roughly five seconds, with subsequent launches effectively instant thanks to mtime-based incremental scanning, and search results in under a millisecond. A full scan is single-pass and does metadata plus FTS in one go.

faq.q: Can another agent read my Wake history?
faq.a: Yes, and that is the most interesting part of the tool. Wake bundles wake-mcp, a read-only MCP server exposing five tools (wake_search, wake_list_sessions, wake_get_session, wake_list_projects, wake_list_memories), plus wake-cli which prints identical output for shells. Add it to Claude Code with `claude mcp add --scope user wake -- "/Applications/Wake.app/Contents/MacOS/wake-mcp"` or to Codex via ~/.codex/config.toml.

faq.q: Do I need Wake running for the MCP server to work?
faq.a: For fresh search and listing results, yes - those come from Wake's index. You can schedule `wake-cli refresh` from launchd or a systemd timer to keep the index current while the app is closed, and every listing reports how recent the index is. Reading a transcript parses the agent's files directly, so it does not depend on the last scan.

faq.q: Can Wake show sessions from my other machines?
faq.a: Yes, via Settings → Remote hosts: Wake probes the remote for known agent directories and mirrors only those with rsync into remotes/<host>/ under its own data directory. Remote sessions are read-only, are searchable with an @host badge, and resume through a copied `ssh -t <host> 'cd <project> && codex resume <id>'` command. SSH must work without prompts, rsync is needed on both ends, and Windows remotes are not supported.

faq.q: Does Wake lose sessions if I delete one?
faq.a: No. Deletion moves the file to the system Trash and records a tombstone in Wake's database, so the session does not reappear after an index rebuild.

faq.q: Can Wake search Chinese, Japanese or Korean text and code snippets?
faq.a: Yes. The FTS5 trigram index handles CJK text and code substrings such as `useEffect(` in the same query, and a result opens the transcript at the matched message rather than dumping you at the top of a file.

faq.q: Does Wake use AI or embeddings to search?
faq.a: No. It is a literal full-text index (FTS5 with trigram tokenisation), deliberately not a summarisation or embedding layer. If you need semantic recall on paraphrased queries, that is where ctx's optional local semantic mode, valpere/session-indexer (bge-m3 via Ollama) or TheSylvester/crispy-recall differ.
